question: Through a fuzz pedal, rock guitarists play two-note power chords, not full major chords. What goes wrong with the third note?
answer: Distortion invents notes at the sums and differences of the frequencies going in. A guitar's fifth is a fiftieth of a semitone from a pure 3:2, so the new tones join the root's family. Its major third is a seventh of a semitone off 5:4, so its new tones land off and beat: mud.
move: An ingredient that works alone can spoil once the heat is turned up.
ask: What works well in small doses in my life but turns to noise when I turn it up?

scene.hint: Tap keys to build chords, then picture each one through a fuzz pedal.

moments.name: Power chord
moments.text: Distortion adds B minus E, 41 Hz: an E an octave lower. It fits the chord.

moments.name: Bare fifth
moments.text: Almost exactly 3 : 2, so every tone distortion adds is a cousin of E.

moments.name: Major chord
moments.text: This G# is a seventh of a semitone sharp of 5 : 4. Through fuzz, it beats.

moments.name: Minor chord
moments.text: Its third misses 6 : 5 by about as much. Through fuzz, mud again.

reference: Esa Lilja, Dealing with the 3rd: Anatomy of distorted chords and subsequent compositional features in classic heavy metal, in Karjalainen & Kärki (eds), Modern Heavy Metal: Markets, Practices and Cultures, Aalto University, 2015, pp. 393-403; equal-tempered fifth 700 cents against 702, major third 400 against 386 (arithmetic)
